catalog_citation: Ingram, Andrew. 2001. Anamuxra: a language of Madang Province, Papua New Guinea. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, University of Sydney. 437 pp. Open access: Sydney eScholarship hdl:2123/9823; copy read from COREhttps://core.ac.uk/download/41237500.pdf.
catalog_locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, §2.5 'Stress', pp. 51-53: rule (R-11) with footnote 6, examples (2-56)-(2-63); domain sentence §2.1 p. 19; VV nuclei §2.3.3.1 p. 41.
catalog_quote: The rules of stress assignment that account for many phonological words in Anamuxra may be summarised as follows: (R-11) assign stress to a final heavy syllable where heavy syllable equals VV or VC; if there no final heavy syllable, assign stress to the penultimate syllable⁶. [fn. 6: In other words, "stress syllable containing penultimate mora".] Examples of words displaying final stress include: (2-56) a. /aβaβ/ [aβáβ] 'mother's brother' ... f. /arabagin/ [arambaŋgín] 'four days hence' Examples of words bearing penultimate stress include: ... (2-57) a. /ar-pa/ [árpʌ] 'tree-CLres' ... (2-60) a. apapura-pa [ʌpapurápʌ] 'butterfly-CLres' ... Stress associates with underlying vowels wherever possible. Thus, 'target' syllables (i.e. penultimate and final heavy syllables) which contain an epenthetic vowel at surface level are not immediately available to the rules of stress assignment. Rather, stress is assigned to the nearest syllable to the left containing an underlying vowel. In words where there is no underlying vowel to the left of the target syllable then the closest syllable to the right is selected. ... There are cases of discrepancies between the surface realisation of stress and the stress rules outlined above. One such case are verbs inflected for third person singular subject and near tense take antepenultimate stress. ... The stress assignment found in third person singular subject forms of verbs marked for near tense is clearly morphologically driven.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable if it is heavy (long vowel/diphthong VV or closed VC), otherwise on the penult — equivalently, on the syllable containing the penultimate mora. Epenthetic vowels cannot bear stress: if the target syllable has an epenthetic vowel, stress goes to the nearest syllable to its left with an underlying vowel (or to the right if none exists to the left). Examples: [aβáβ] 'mother's brother', [arambaŋgín] 'four days hence' (final heavy) vs [árpʌ] 'tree-CL', [βuɣasírpʌ] 'spider-CL', [ʌpapurápʌ] 'butterfly-CL' (penult).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; the thesis speaks only of a single primary stress per phonological word (compounds, noun+article/demonstrative, serialised verbs and bound pronominals form one phonological word with one primary stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Author says the rule accounts for 'many' (not all) phonological words. Explicit exception: verbs inflected for near tense with 3sg subject take antepenultimate stress ([dáriya] 'hear-NT-3SGS', [támiya], [tór iya]) versus regular [darína] 'hear-NT-2SGS', [torín] 'hold-NT-1SGS' — 'clearly morphologically driven'. Epenthetic-vowel syllables are skipped ([índəpa] 'fishing spear-CL', [mátɨkəpa] 'crocodile-CL', [səɣʌ́] 'again').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stem plus classifier/inflectional suffixes and incorporated bound forms); examples are citation forms of inflected words. Description based mainly on the Waiateng ('southern') dialect where Ingram did most fieldwork, with data also from Ikundun and Mindivi; no dialect differences in stress are mentioned.
new_statements.identity_note: Ingram's 'Anamuxra' = Glottolog anam1248 / ISO imi, the language earlier called Ikundun (Z'graggen) in the Josephstaal (Pomoikan) group; Ingram distinguishes a northern dialect (Mindivi, Ikundun, Tuamadapuar) and a southern dialect (Apovd, Swanzambi, Waiateng); his data come chiefly from Waiateng (southern) with some Ikundun and Mindivi material. No stress differences between dialects are reported.

sources.note: The Introduction (section 3, p. vi) states that Isabi and Biyom (Brahman group) are tonal and are the only tonal languages so far known within the Adelbert Range language group - i.e. Z'graggen did not observe tone in the Josephstaal/Southern Adelbert languages he lists, Ikundun among them; section 9 (p. ix) says the transcription is 'semi-phonemic' and lists sound fluctuations per language (Ikundun: l ~ r) with no stress or tone marking; the Ikundun material itself is a c. 300-item wordlist plus pronoun/number-marking/verb-inflection notes. No per-language prosodic statement.
